I am working on my PhD thesis and I need help putting together the literature review section for Chapter 2, which focuses on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In my workspace there is a compressed archive called research_notes.tar.gz that contains some preliminary notes I have been keeping in markdown files about background concepts, key research questions, and related retrieval methods. I would appreciate it if you could first extract that archive so we can see what is in there, and then read through the notes to understand the context of my research.

My research focus and the key concepts I am tracking are stored in a knowledge graph file located at memory/memory.json in the workspace. Please read that to understand the scope and direction of my literature review.

After familiarizing yourself with my notes and research focus, I need you to search academic databases for recent and foundational papers on Retrieval-Augmented Generation. I am looking for approximately five key papers that cover the topic from different angles, including the original RAG formulation, survey papers, self-reflective retrieval approaches, recursive retrieval methods, and practical system-building perspectives. For each paper you find, please download it and read through its content to understand the main contributions. I would also like you to look at the source manuscripts of these papers to examine the methodology sections in more detail, since the methodology comparison is an important part of my literature review.

Once you have gathered all of this information, please store the key findings in my knowledge graph so that I can reference them later. Then create a Word document called Literature_Review.docx in my workspace. The document should begin with an introduction section that provides an overview of Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a research area and explains why it matters for knowledge-intensive natural language processing tasks. Following the introduction, include a dedicated section for each of the five papers you found. Each paper section should clearly state the paper title, the authors, the publication year, a description of the main contribution, and a discussion of the methodology used. After covering all five papers, end the document with a conclusion section that synthesizes the key themes, identifies common patterns across the papers, and suggests directions for future research. Please make sure the writing flows naturally and reads like a proper academic literature review rather than a collection of disconnected summaries.

A few things to keep in mind while you work.

First, the databases may return papers that are not actually about Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including papers from other fields. Judge each result by its title and abstract. The review should cover only the papers that are genuinely about RAG; please do not include or discuss unrelated papers in Literature_Review.docx.

Second, the deliverable is a single file, Literature_Review.docx, and it must end up complete and well-formed. It must be created exactly once, by exactly one designated agent, and only after all of the paper content has been gathered. Any agent that is responsible for only a portion of this task (for example, researching a subset of the papers) must NOT create, write, overwrite, or append to Literature_Review.docx; that agent should instead return its findings in its report or write them to its own separately named intermediate file that no other agent writes to. Do not have several agents append to or rewrite the same document file, as that will corrupt or overwrite it. A safe way to work in parallel is to have each agent take responsibility for a distinct subset of the papers and return its findings, and then have one agent assemble the final document exactly once, after all of the findings are in.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, use exactly one research wave. The main agent must extract `research_notes.tar.gz` once without overwriting files, read the extracted Markdown and `memory/memory.json`, and freeze these five non-overlapping topics: original RAG formulation; RAG survey; self-reflective/adaptive retrieval; recursive/hierarchical retrieval; and practical system building.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents in parallel:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Explore 0 owns only the original RAG formulation topic.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Explore 1 owns only the strongest RAG survey topic.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Explore 2 owns only self-reflective or adaptive retrieval.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Explore 3 owns only recursive or hierarchical retrieval.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Explore 4 owns only practical RAG system building.

Each explore sub-agent searches only its assigned topic, rejects off-topic titles/abstracts, selects exactly one distinct paper, downloads and reads that paper, inspects the available LaTeX methodology sections, and writes one uniquely named compact evidence JSON containing topic, stable ID, exact title, authors, year, contribution, methodology, evidence section names, and limitations. Return only the JSON path, stable ID, and compact search/read controls. No sub-agent may modify the knowledge graph or create `Literature_Review.docx`.

After Wave 1, the main agent verifies five distinct IDs and five topic slots, then directly owns both remaining outputs. Update the existing knowledge graph by adding only the five source-supported paper entities and relationships while preserving unrelated nodes. Create `Literature_Review.docx` exactly once with one bulk structured write: title; Introduction; five sections in the frozen topic order, each stating the exact title, authors, year, main contribution, and methodology; and a synthetic Conclusion with common themes and future research. Use only the five retained papers, exclude all rejected results, read the graph and document back once, and finish without another sub-agent or verification wave.

/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/Literature_Review.docx

You are the ONLY agent that writes to this file. Do not ask anyone else to modify it, and do not create any other copies. If the file already exists, overwrite it cleanly by creating it fresh (create_document). Use the Word MCP tools (mcp__word__create_document, mcp__word__add_heading, mcp__word__add_paragraph, mcp__word__add_page_break as needed). The document must end up complete and well-formed.

CONTEXT: This is Chapter 2 (Literature Review) of a PhD thesis on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The thesis investigates: (a) how retrieval mechanisms can supply the most relevant context for knowledge-intensive generation, considering both quality and efficiency; (b) the relationship between retrieval granularity (sentence/paragraph/document/summary level) and generation quality; and (c) evaluation of RAG systems — beyond end-task accuracy toward attribution quality, retrieval relevance, and faithfulness to retrieved sources. The review must cover exactly five papers, all genuinely about RAG (do NOT add any other papers — in particular there are unrelated papers in storage about medical image segmentation, quantum computing, robotics RL, and GNNs that must NOT appear in this document).

WRITING STYLE REQUIREMENTS: Write flowing, coherent academic prose that reads like a proper literature review, not a collection of disconnected summaries. Use transition sentences to connect papers thematically (e.g., how the survey's taxonomy frames the later work, how Self-RAG and RAPTOR respond to limitations of the original retrieve-then-read pipeline, how the practical paper operationalizes design choices). Each paper section should integrate the paper's contribution and methodology into the broader narrative of the chapter. Use professional academic tone.

DOCUMENT STRUCTURE (use Heading 1 for the main sections; you may use Heading 2 within paper sections for "Contribution" / "Methodology" if it aids readability, but flowing paragraphs are preferred):

1. Title heading: "Chapter 2: Literature Review — Retrieval-Augmented Generation" (or similar).

2. "Introduction" — A substantial introduction (several paragraphs) giving an overview of RAG as a research area: the combination of parametric knowledge (in LLM weights) with non-parametric knowledge (external retrieval), why it matters for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks (open-domain QA, fact verification, long-document reasoning), how it addresses hallucination, stale knowledge, and non-transparent reasoning. Motivate the thesis themes: retrieval relevance and efficiency, retrieval granularity vs generation quality, and the need for richer evaluation. End by previewing the five papers and the structure of the chapter.

3. Five paper sections, in this order (each section must clearly state the paper TITLE, AUTHORS, PUBLICATION YEAR, MAIN CONTRIBUTION, and a discussion of METHODOLOGY):

Section A — Lewis et al. (2020): "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (arXiv:2005.11401; NeurIPS 2020).
- Authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Kuttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktaschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela.
- Contribution: the original RAG formulation; a general-purpose fine-tuning recipe combining a parametric memory (pre-trained seq2seq BART) with a non-parametric memory (dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed via the DPR neural retriever).
- Methodology: joint end-to-end training by marginalizing over retrieved documents when computing generation likelihood; two variants — RAG-Sequence (same retrieved document conditions the whole output sequence) and RAG-Token (different documents can condition each token), which is precisely a retrieval-granularity axis; single-shot retrieve-then-read, no iteration or self-reflection. Evaluation on four knowledge-intensive tasks (open-domain QA incl. Natural Questions, abstractive QA, Jeopardy question generation, fact verification), exact match metric; 44.5 EM on Natural Questions, then state of the art. Note that evaluation is end-task accuracy only (no attribution/faithfulness metrics) — a point the thesis critiques.

Section B — Gao et al. (2023): "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey" (arXiv:2312.10997; arXiv preprint).
- Authors: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan, Yuxi Bi, Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun, Haofen Wang.
- Contribution: comprehensive survey organizing RAG into three paradigms — Naive RAG (retrieve-read-generate), Advanced RAG (pre-retrieval and post-retrieval optimizations such as query rewriting, re-ranking, context compression), and Modular RAG (flexible composition of retrieval, generation, and augmentation modules) — plus RAG infrastructure and evaluation methods.
- Methodology: literature taxonomy comparing 50+ recent papers along retrieval strategies, augmentation methods, and generation quality; surveys evaluation benchmarks (RGB, RECALL, CRUD) and identifies key evaluation dimensions: relevance, faithfulness, answer correctness. This frames the design space (rewriting, re-ranking, compression, modular composition) that subsequent papers explore.

Section C — Asai et al. (2024): "Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection" (arXiv:2402.19473; ICLR 2024).
- Authors: Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil, Hannaneh Hajishirzi.
- Contribution: trains a single arbitrary LM to adaptively retrieve passages on demand, generate from retrieved passages, and reflect on its own generation using special reflection tokens — addressing the problem that fixed retrieve-always pipelines can degrade quality when retrieval is unnecessary or irrelevant.
- Methodology: four reflection tokens — Retrieve (decides whether retrieval is needed), ISREL (assesses relevance of retrieved passages), ISSUP (checks whether generation is supported by the passage), ISUSE (evaluates overall utility of the response); a critic model generates reflection-token annotations used to fine-tune the generator, distilling critique into the LM; at inference the model emits tokens to trigger retrieval on demand and self-assess outputs, improving both quality and efficiency. Evaluated on six tasks (open-domain QA, reasoning, fact verification); e.g., PopQA 54.9 accuracy vs 44.0 for ChatGPT and 51.2 for standard RAG. Retrieval is passage-level; the reflection tokens operationalize evaluation of relevance/support/utility — relevant to the thesis's evaluation thread.

Section D — Sarthi et al. (2024): "RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval" (arXiv:2310.11511; ICLR 2024).
- Authors: Parth Sarthi, Salman Abdullah, Aditi Tuli, Shubh Khanna, Anna Goldie, Christopher D. Manning.
- Contribution: a tree-based retrieval system that recursively embeds, clusters, and summarizes text chunks to build a bottom-up tree of summaries at differing levels of abstraction, overcoming the limitation of retrieving only short contiguous chunks which misses holistic, whole-document understanding.
- Methodology: leaf nodes are text chunks; Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering groups the chunk embeddings; an LLM summarizes each cluster into a parent node; the embed-cluster-summarize process recurses to a root, creating multi-granularity representations; at inference, retrieval runs either as top-down tree traversal or as a flat "collapsed tree" search across all levels, offering context at multiple abstraction levels. Evaluated on NarrativeQA and QASPER; on NarrativeQA, RAPTOR with GPT-4 achieves METEOR 30.87 vs 23.52 for standard chunk retrieval — direct evidence that retrieval granularity affects generation quality. Evaluation uses an end-task metric (METEOR) rather than retrieval-side metrics.

Section E — Chen et al. (2024): "From RAG to Rich: Building Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems" (arXiv:2404.10981; arXiv preprint).
- Authors: Wenqi Chen, Jialin Wu, Dawei Zhu, Xiaoguang Li, Shuaiyi Nie.
- Contribution: a practical, engineering-oriented framework for building robust production RAG systems across the full lifecycle from data ingestion to deployment and monitoring, bridging research prototypes and production deployment.
- Methodology: organizes RAG design into five pillars — data ingestion (parsing, chunking, metadata), indexing (embedding selection, vector database, hybrid dense+BM25 search), retrieval pipeline (query understanding, multi-stage retrieval, re-ranking), generation (prompt engineering, context window management, citation generation), and evaluation (automated metrics, human evaluation, regression testing). Empirically, ablation studies across legal, medical, and technical documentation domains quantify the impact of design choices: chunking strategy has the largest effect on retrieval quality (up to 23% improvement), followed by embedding choice (15%) and re-ranking (12%); hybrid dense+sparse search consistently outperforms either alone. No model training; contribution is configuration/engineering guidance. Chunking as a first-class design variable is effectively a retrieval-granularity decision.

4. "Conclusion" — Synthesize the key themes across the five papers: the evolution from a fixed retrieve-then-read pipeline (Lewis) to a structured taxonomy of optimizations (Gao) to adaptive, self-reflective retrieval (Asai) and hierarchical, multi-granularity retrieval (Sarthi), and finally to engineering practices for robust systems (Chen). Identify common patterns: (i) the central role of retrieval quality and relevance for generation success; (ii) retrieval granularity as a recurring design lever (RAG-Sequence vs RAG-Token, chunking in Chen, multi-level tree abstraction in RAPTOR); (iii) the trend toward adaptivity and self-assessment rather than static pipelines; (iv) evaluation still dominated by end-task metrics with a growing call for richer dimensions (relevance, faithfulness, attribution — as in the Gao survey's dimensions and Self-RAG's reflection tokens). Suggest directions for future research that connect to the thesis questions: learned/adaptive retrieval policies, principled handling of retrieval granularity, hybrid evaluation frameworks that capture attribution and faithfulness, and transferring production lessons (hybrid search, re-ranking, monitoring) back into research systems.

FINAL CHECKS before you finish:
- The file must exist at the exact path given above and be a valid .docx.
- It must contain the Introduction, five paper sections, and Conclusion.
- Only the five RAG papers above may be discussed; no unrelated papers.
- Verify by reading back the document text (mcp__word__get_document_text) and confirm structure (mcp__word__get_document_outline), then report: the exact file path, the document's section headings, and confirmation that all required parts are present.
